messages.subject: Beginner questions
parts:
Hi, I've just finished watching the variogram and home range tutorials on Animove and am still wrapping my head around the subject (thank you so much for supplying such helpful educational tools). I successfully ran the code on a couple test individuals and now want to get the analysis underway on my entire dataset (n  = 23 individuals, 74k locations).

I have a few fundamental questions I was hoping you could assist with to help get me underway please. 
  1. Some individuals are seasonal migrants but only spend ~3 months away from their breeding home ranges (so range-resident 9 months of the year). Is there any issue with limiting the timespan of analysis to the breeding season to increase the study sample size by including these migrants?
  2. Pertaining to question above - some individuals were also tagged as juveniles and either commenced breeding in second-third year or appeared to establish a home range by year 2. Prior to this they dispersed widely and meandered during their first-year. Can I subset these individuals from their first-year onwards to disregard juvenile movements or will the variogram pick up range-residency after this time period anyways and I can include these individuals in home range analysis?
  3. Most of the tracking data is GPS data with a regular sampling schedule, but a smaller proportion are satellite (Argos) data with an irregular sampling schedule. Just checking that by treating these data individually (e.g. use weighted AKDE for satellite data but defaults for GPS) that home range estimates will still be comparable?
  4. Is it possible/acceptable to calculate home ranges per individual per year? We have had individuals shift territories (e.g. breeding females swapping partners) between years, and also have interesting analysis to do regarding potential home range size shift for individuals in areas undergoing habitat loss (e.g. is home range size increasing as useable space decreases?) which would necessitate annual home range calculation. 
Once again, thank you.
Chris

messages.author: 7d868ffe3daa8319
messages.subject: Re: [ctmm-user] Beginner questions
parts:
Hi Chris,

1. It depends on what you want (biologically) out of your (statistical) home range estimate. If you want to calculate area requirements, for example, cutting out the migratory period would clearly underestimate the area needed by the migratory animals. If you want to compare the areas used by a set of animals in a protected area, though, this might be fine.

2. You should subset to times when an animal has a stationary (unchanging) movement pattern. An assumption of AKDE right now is that an animal's movement pattern is the same across the entire time period of the training data, so including time periods when an animal is doing something different can create a bad statistical estimate.

3. We recommend always using the weighted AKDE unless it is computationally infeasible. But yes, one advantage of AKDEs is that they are comparable across all kinds of different data. That is often/usually not true of other estimators.

4. Again, because an assumption of the AKDE model is that an animal has a stationary movement pattern, if the animal is doing something different from year to year, then you should be subsetting by year. If the animal is maintaining a stationary home range, the estimates between years will essentially overlap and small differences in the home range will not be biologically meaningful.

Hope this is helpful.

Jesse
